articles.text: immediate hazard assessment practical introductory reference for immediate hazard assessment. emergency survival & decision making check for fire, floodwater, damaged electrical equipment, unstable structures, and hazardous air. move to a safer location when the route is clear. call emergency services when available and follow local instructions. account for everyone and reassess as conditions change.

shelter or evacuate decision practical introductory reference for shelter or evacuate decision. emergency survival & decision making check current evacuation orders and immediate threats. identify safe shelter options and accessible evacuation routes. consider household medical, mobility, and communication needs. leave early when directed; do not enter flooded roads.

household accountability practical introductory reference for household accountability. emergency survival & decision making use a printed roster and identify everyone in the household. record last known safe locations and contact methods. choose a meeting point and an alternate. share status through available communications and update the roster.

incident information log practical introductory reference for incident information log. emergency survival & decision making record the date, time, location, source, and observed conditions. separate verified observations from reports and assumptions. note decisions, actions, and outstanding needs. keep a paper copy when device power is uncertain.

safe water priorities practical introductory reference for safe water priorities. water collection & treatment use commercially bottled water when available. follow local boil water and do not drink advisories. keep untreated water separate from drinking water. if chemical contamination is suspected, boiling does not make the water safe.

water storage and rotation practical introductory reference for water storage and rotation. water collection & treatment use clean food grade containers with secure lids. label containers with the filling date and source. store away from fuel, pesticides, and direct sunlight. inspect containers and follow public health guidance for replacement.

boil water advisory response practical introductory reference for boil water advisory response. water collection & treatment check the exact local advisory and affected area. follow the public health agency's boiling instructions and duration. use safe water for drinking, food preparation, and oral hygiene. wait for the official all clear before resuming normal use.

water contamination warning signs practical introductory reference for water contamination warning signs. water collection & treatment treat floodwater and water from damaged systems as potentially unsafe. do not rely on appearance, smell, or taste to establish safety. chemical contamination requires specific guidance; boiling may worsen concentration. consult the water utility or public health authority for approved alternatives.

first aid scene safety practical introductory reference for first aid scene safety. medical care & first aid check the scene for hazards before approaching. call emergency services and request an aed when indicated. use gloves or other protective barriers when available. provide care within your training and follow dispatcher instructions.

severe bleeding response practical introductory reference for severe bleeding response. medical care & first aid call emergency services immediately. apply firm direct pressure with a clean dressing. for life threatening limb bleeding, use a tourniquet if trained and one is available. monitor the person and follow emergency dispatcher instructions.

heat illness recognition practical introductory reference for heat illness recognition. medical care & first aid move the person away from heat and begin cooling. confusion, collapse, or altered consciousness may indicate heat stroke. call emergency services immediately for suspected heat stroke. do not give fluids by mouth to a person who cannot safely swallow.

medication continuity planning practical introductory reference for medication continuity planning. medical care & first aid maintain an up to date medication list with doses and prescriber contacts. keep medicines in their required storage conditions. ask a pharmacist about emergency refills and storage during outages. do not change prescriptions without qualified medical advice.

shelter site selection practical introductory reference for shelter site selection. shelter & environmental protection avoid floodplains, unstable trees, damaged structures, and downed lines. check ventilation, weather protection, and safe exits. keep combustion devices outside living and sleeping spaces. plan for accessibility, sanitation, and communication.

carbon monoxide prevention practical introductory reference for carbon monoxide prevention. shelter & environmental protection never run generators, grills, or fuel burning equipment indoors or in garages. position generators outside and away from openings according to manufacturer guidance. use functioning carbon monoxide alarms. if an alarm sounds or poisoning is suspected, move outdoors and call emergency services.

cold weather protection practical introductory reference for cold weather protection. shelter & environmental protection seek dry shelter and change wet clothing. layer clothing and protect the head, hands, and feet. watch for confusion, unusual drowsiness, or impaired coordination. seek emergency care for suspected hypothermia.

family communications plan practical introductory reference for family communications plan. radio & emergency communications identify primary and alternate contact methods. choose an out of area contact and household meeting locations. write down contact information and check in procedures. practice the plan and keep paper copies.

radio message logging practical introductory reference for radio message logging. radio & emergency communications record time, station, sender, recipient, and message content. use plain language and confirm critical details. mark unverified reports clearly. protect personal information and follow applicable radio rules.

communications power resilience practical introductory reference for communications power resilience. radio & emergency communications charge devices and battery packs before forecast hazards. identify compatible cables, spare batteries, and low power modes. use radios only within their intended operating and licensing requirements. plan for communication failures and in person check ins.

power outage priorities practical introductory reference for power outage priorities. power generation & electricity identify critical medical equipment and refrigeration needs. use battery powered lighting rather than candles where practical. keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed. follow utility instructions and report downed lines.

generator safety overview practical introductory reference for generator safety overview. power generation & electricity operate portable generators outdoors only. keep exhaust away from doors, windows, and vents. use properly rated cords and follow manufacturer instructions. never backfeed household wiring through a wall outlet.

battery and charging plan practical introductory reference for battery and charging plan. power generation & electricity inventory device power requirements and charging connectors. prioritize communications, medical, and lighting needs. store batteries according to manufacturer guidance. inspect damaged or swollen batteries and stop using them.

evacuation go bag practical introductory reference for evacuation go bag. family & household continuity pack essential medicines, identification, contact lists, and chargers. include water, suitable food, clothing, and basic hygiene items. account for children, pets, and accessibility needs. review contents and expiration dates regularly.

household document backup practical introductory reference for household document backup. family & household continuity maintain secure copies of identification, insurance, and key records. keep an offline copy protected from unauthorized access. store a paper contact sheet separately. review documents after major household changes.

pet evacuation preparation practical introductory reference for pet evacuation preparation. family & household continuity prepare carriers, leashes, food, water, and veterinary records. identify pet friendly evacuation options in advance. keep identification and contact information current. never leave animals in unsafe heat or flood conditions.

return home after disaster practical introductory reference for return home after disaster. family & household continuity wait for official clearance before returning. avoid standing water, damaged wiring, unstable structures, and suspected gas leaks. photograph damage only when safe. use qualified professionals for hazardous repairs.

household emergency supply inventory a basic inventory procedure for recording and reviewing household emergency supplies. family & household continuity choose a single inventory location, such as a printed sheet or a locally stored document. record each supply item, quantity, storage location, and expiration date when applicable. identify supplies that are missing, damaged, or nearing expiration. review the inventory on a recurring schedule and update it after supplies are used. keep a printed copy accessible when electricity or internet access is unavailable.

emergency go bag inventory build and maintain a portable collection of essential supplies for a short notice evacuation. family & household continuity identify each household member’s essential needs, including mobility, communication, medications, and infant or pet supplies. choose a bag that each intended carrier can lift and transport safely. avoid making the bag so heavy that it slows evacuation. pack drinking water, shelf stable food, a flashlight, spare batteries, a power bank, basic first aid supplies, hygiene items, and weather appropriate clothing. include copies of essential contact information and documents, protected against water and unauthorized access. add a paper map, a whistle, and a small amount of cash in appropriate denominations. check expiration dates, battery charge, clothing sizes, and changing medical needs on a recurring schedule. store the bag in a known accessible location and make sure household members know where it is.

household emergency contact card prepare a compact contact and reunification reference that works without a phone. family & household continuity write the names and phone numbers of primary caregivers, local emergency contacts, and one contact outside the affected region. identify a nearby meeting location and a separate location outside the neighborhood, accounting for accessibility needs. include relevant medical alert information only when necessary and protect sensitive information from casual disclosure. provide each household member with a paper copy appropriate to their age and circumstances. agree on a simple procedure for reporting safety and location when communications are available. review the card whenever contact numbers, schools, workplaces, or household needs change.

safe flashlight and battery readiness maintain safe portable lighting during a power outage. power generation & electricity place a working flashlight or headlamp in each important household location and keep a spare accessible. use the battery chemistry and charging equipment specified by the manufacturer. inspect battery compartments for corrosion, swelling, leaks, or heat damage. do not use damaged cells. charge rechargeable devices ahead of forecast disruptions and periodically test their operation. keep spare batteries in their original packaging or protected holders so terminals cannot short together. use battery powered lighting rather than candles where possible to reduce fire risk. do not charge damaged lithium ion batteries or leave charging equipment in unsafe locations.

refrigerator and freezer outage log track power interruptions and food temperature to support safer food decisions. food & nutrition record the time the power failed and the last known refrigerator and freezer temperatures if available. keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as practical to slow warming. use an appliance thermometer to measure temperatures rather than judging food by smell or appearance. follow current usda or local public health guidance for time and temperature limits before deciding whether to keep perishable food. when in doubt about the safety of perishable food, discard it. do not taste food to determine safety. record when power returned and any food discarded or moved to another safe cold storage location.

boil water advisory response respond to an official boil water advisory without confusing it with a do not drink notice. water collection & treatment confirm the exact notice and affected area using the water utility or local public health authority. identify whether the notice is a boil water advisory, a do not drink notice, or a do not use notice. boiling does not remove chemical contaminants. for a boil water advisory concerning microbial contamination, bring clear water to a full rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes at elevations above 6,500 feet, unless the issuing authority directs otherwise. if water is cloudy, first filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter or allow particles to settle and pour off the clear water. let boiled water cool in a clean, covered container. use treated or approved bottled water for drinking, preparing food, and brushing teeth as directed. follow the issuing authority’s specific instructions for infant formula, medical devices, dishwashing, and pets. only resume normal use after the authority officially lifts the notice and follow any flushing instructions.

home utility shutoff reference document household utility controls before an emergency. family & household continuity locate the main water shutoff, electrical service disconnect, and gas meter or shutoff without operating them unnecessarily. photograph or sketch each location and record access instructions in a protected household reference. ask the utility or a qualified professional which controls occupants may safely operate and under what conditions. never approach damaged electrical equipment, standing water near electrical service, or suspected gas leaks to operate a control. if you smell gas or suspect a leak, leave the area and contact the gas utility or emergency services from a safe location. do not operate electrical switches or create sparks. only qualified personnel or the utility should restore gas service after a shutoff. update the reference after repairs, renovations, or changes to utility equipment.

radio communications message log record radio traffic accurately during emergency support activities. radio & emergency communications prepare a paper log with columns for date, local time, station or sender, recipient, message summary, and action taken. identify the radio service and follow applicable licensing, frequency, and operational requirements. listen before transmitting and use concise plain language unless an authorized procedure specifies otherwise. record callsigns and message details accurately. ask for repetition when critical information is unclear. distinguish confirmed information from unverified reports and record the source of each report. avoid transmitting unnecessary personal, medical, or sensitive information over open radio channels. mark tasks completed and retain logs according to the incident organization’s procedures.

floodwater exposure precautions reduce avoidable hazards when floodwater is present. natural disasters & environmental hazards stay out of floodwater whenever possible. floodwater may conceal debris, sewage, sharp objects, and energized equipment. do not drive through flooded roads. turn around and choose a safe alternative route. follow local evacuation orders and avoid entering damaged buildings until officials indicate it is safe. keep children and pets away from standing floodwater and contaminated materials. if contact with floodwater occurs, wash exposed skin with soap and clean water as soon as possible and cover wounds with waterproof dressings. seek medical advice promptly for injuries, signs of infection, or significant exposure involving an open wound. never touch downed power lines or electrical equipment in or near floodwater.

emergency sanitation station set up a temporary hand hygiene and waste management area during a disruption. water, waste & public sanitation choose a location separated from food preparation and drinking water storage. use clean running water and soap for handwashing when available. if unavailable, use an appropriate alcohol based hand sanitizer when hands are not visibly dirty. provide a covered trash container and liners, and keep waste inaccessible to children, animals, and pests. for toilet interruptions, follow local public health and emergency management instructions for approved temporary sanitation arrangements. never discharge untreated waste into streams, wells, storm drains, or drinking water sources. wear appropriate protection when handling contaminated waste and wash hands afterward. inspect the station daily for leaks, overflowing containers, and contamination.

family evacuation departure checklist use a repeatable departure sequence when an evacuation is ordered or necessary. emergency survival & decision making confirm the evacuation order, hazard area, recommended routes, and destination using official local information. account for every household member and arrange assistance for anyone with mobility, medical, or communication needs. take essential medications, identification, emergency contact information, assistive equipment, and available go bags. check vehicle fuel or charge, accessible transport options, road conditions, and a backup route before leaving. notify a trusted contact of the destination and expected check in method when doing so is safe. leave immediately when conditions require it. do not delay for nonessential belongings or routine property preparations. follow official instructions and do not return until authorities indicate it is safe.

emergency contact and reunification plan create a plan that works when family members are separated and phones fail. family & household continuity list every household member and their usual locations during the day. choose two meeting places: one immediately outside the home and one outside the neighborhood. choose an out of area contact who can relay short status messages. write each person’s phone numbers, relevant accessibility needs, and pickup permissions on a paper card. agree on who retrieves children, who checks on dependent adults, and how to report a change of plan. practice the plan, including an exercise without mobile data. store copies in bags, vehicles, and a protected household folder. safety note: do not publish sensitive personal details in the shared library.

household hazard walk through identify preventable household hazards before a disruption. emergency survival & decision making walk each room and identify blocked exits, unsecured heavy furniture, damaged cords, and overloaded outlets. check that smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are installed and working according to manufacturer instructions. locate water, gas, and electrical shutoff controls and document who is qualified to operate them. inspect exterior drainage, trees, loose objects, and access routes without entering unsafe areas. prioritize hazards by potential severity and ease of correction. record actions, responsible person, and completion date. repeat after major repairs, storms, or household changes. safety note: never touch damaged electrical equipment or investigate suspected gas leaks. leave the area and contact appropriate responders.

emergency kit inspection cycle maintain emergency supplies through recurring inspection. family & household continuity create an inventory listing item, quantity, location, expiration date, and condition. separate essential daily medications and items that require special handling from general supplies. check flashlights, radio batteries, chargers, and cables using their normal operating procedures. inspect sealed food and water for damaged containers and follow manufacturer storage instructions. replace expired or damaged items and record the replacement date. check clothing and footwear sizes for children. set a recurring calendar reminder and repeat after using the kit. safety note: follow medication storage guidance; do not substitute expired or damaged medicines based on this checklist.

safe flashlight and battery use use portable lighting while reducing fire and battery hazards. power generation & electricity prefer purpose built led flashlights or lanterns over open flames. check device and battery labels for compatible chemistry, size, and charging requirements. inspect for swelling, leakage, corrosion, heat, or damage before use. keep spare batteries protected against short circuits and away from heat and moisture. use manufacturer approved charging equipment and a stable, ventilated charging surface. assign lights to fixed locations and verify each light works during periodic inspections. recycle damaged batteries through an appropriate collection program. safety note: do not charge swollen or damaged batteries; avoid mixing incompatible battery types.

refrigerator and freezer outage log track temperature and time during a power interruption. food & nutrition record the time power was lost and the last known safe appliance temperatures. keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as practical. use appliance thermometers to measure actual temperatures when available. record each opening, observed temperature, and time on a paper log. consult current usda or local public health guidance before deciding which perishable foods to retain. discard food when safety is uncertain; smell and appearance cannot establish safety. clean and dry the appliance after spoiled food is removed. safety note: food safety thresholds depend on measured temperature and elapsed time; verify current usda guidance.

paper communications message form record accurate messages for handoff when networks are unreliable. radio & emergency communications start a log with date, local time, time zone, station or sender identifier, and operator name. for each message record recipient, sender, priority, exact text, and the time received. read back critical names, numbers, locations, and instructions to confirm accuracy. mark messages as pending, delivered, or unable to deliver, including the time and method. use plain language and avoid transmitting sensitive personal information unnecessarily. preserve original entries; correct mistakes with an annotated update rather than silently erasing. transfer completed logs to the designated records custodian. safety note: transmit only on frequencies and services for which you are authorized; do not treat unverified reports as confirmed.

household water storage inventory track stored water without assuming unknown water is potable. water collection & treatment list each container, its volume, fill date, source, and storage location. use containers intended for drinking water and follow their cleaning instructions. keep containers sealed and protected from heat, sunlight, fuel, and chemicals. inspect for damage, leaks, unusual odor, or contamination before use. record household water needs, including pets and medical or accessibility requirements. maintain a separate label for water that is not verified safe for drinking. follow current local health authority instructions during boil water or do not drink advisories. safety note: boiling does not remove chemical contamination; follow the specific advisory and use an alternative safe supply when instructed.

shelter room selection checklist identify safer interior refuge options for different hazards. shelter & environmental protection identify the specific hazard before selecting a room; flood, tornado, smoke, and extreme heat require different actions. consult local emergency management guidance for designated shelters and evacuation orders. for tornado risk, identify a small interior room on the lowest suitable level, away from windows, when no rated safe room is available. for flood risk, avoid basements and low areas and follow evacuation instructions. verify exits, communication options, accessibility, and space for all household members. stage a flashlight, shoes, communications device, and essential supplies. practice reaching the selected area without relying on electricity. safety note: a single room is not safe for every hazard; do not shelter in a flood prone basement.

storm debris documentation document property damage without entering unsafe areas. emergency management & community response wait until officials indicate it is safe to access the property. photograph visible damage from safe positions before cleanup where practical. record date, location, approximate dimensions, and affected property for each item. keep receipts for emergency repairs, lodging, and necessary supplies. separate debris by local collection rules without touching downed lines or unknown chemicals. use appropriate protective equipment for permitted cleanup tasks. back up photos and notes locally and keep a paper summary for insurance or assistance applications. safety note: avoid unstable structures, floodwater, exposed wiring, and suspicious containers; request professional assistance.

evacuation departure checklist use a repeatable process to leave promptly when instructed. emergency survival & decision making check official evacuation instructions and the latest route restrictions. account for household members and confirm the destination and alternate destination. pack essential medicines, identification, accessibility equipment, pet supplies, and communications devices. notify the designated contact of departure and intended route without sharing sensitive details publicly. secure the home only if doing so does not delay a required evacuation. record departure time, vehicle fuel level, and planned check in points. avoid flooded roads and obey road closure instructions. safety note: do not delay evacuation to complete a checklist or retrieve property.

generator placement and carbon monoxide precautions reduce lethal exhaust and electrical hazards from portable generators. power generation & electricity read the generator manual and identify its exhaust outlet before operation. operate portable fuel powered generators outdoors only, well away from doors, windows, vents, and occupied structures. never operate a generator in a garage, basement, enclosed porch, or near an opening, even with doors open. use working carbon monoxide alarms inside occupied buildings. keep the generator dry and follow manufacturer instructions for cords and connected loads. never connect a generator to household wiring without properly installed transfer equipment by a qualified electrician. shut down and allow cooling before refueling according to the manufacturer. safety note: carbon monoxide is odorless and can kill quickly. if an alarm sounds or symptoms develop, move everyone to fresh air and seek emergency help.

smoke alarm response and exit drill practice rapid exit when a smoke alarm activates. fire, heating & cooking systems identify two ways out of each sleeping area where possible. keep exit paths clear and agree on an outdoor meeting point. test alarms according to the manufacturer and local requirements. practice exiting low under smoke during drills without creating smoke or fire. if an alarm sounds, leave immediately and close doors behind you when safe. once outside, call emergency services and report anyone missing. never reenter a burning building. safety note: do not spend time collecting belongings or attempt to investigate a growing fire.

extreme heat household check plan coordinate safe check ins during dangerous heat. natural disasters & environmental hazards monitor official heat alerts and local cooling center announcements. identify people who may need extra help, including older adults, young children, and those without reliable cooling. agree on check in times and backup communication methods. identify a safe, accessible cooled location and a transport plan. keep drinking water available and follow individual medical advice about fluid restrictions. recognize confusion, fainting, and other signs of severe heat illness as reasons for urgent medical help. document missed check ins and activate the agreed escalation plan. safety note: heat stroke is a medical emergency. call emergency services for altered mental status or other severe symptoms.

emergency sanitation station setup organize hand hygiene and waste handling when normal plumbing is interrupted. water, waste & public sanitation determine whether public health or utility officials have issued sewage or water restrictions. separate handwashing, food preparation, and waste handling areas. provide soap and a safe water source for handwashing when available. use lined, closable waste containers and keep them away from food and children. follow local public health instructions for toilet alternatives and waste disposal. wear suitable gloves for handling waste and wash hands afterward. inspect the station regularly and replenish supplies. safety note: do not discharge waste into floodwater, waterways, or storm drains; local rules govern disposal.

medication and medical equipment continuity list document essential health supplies for an evacuation or outage. family & household continuity create a private list of prescribed medicines, dose instructions from the label, prescriber, and pharmacy contact. list equipment that depends on electricity, refrigeration, consumables, or routine servicing. ask the treating clinician or pharmacist about safe backup arrangements and travel storage. identify charging and backup power needs from device manuals. keep essential documentation accessible to authorized caregivers. review the list after medication or equipment changes. protect records from unauthorized access and keep an offline copy. safety note: do not change medication doses or use improvised power connections based on this list.

neighborhood welfare check coordination organize voluntary checks without creating additional risk. emergency management & community response confirm whether local emergency management has issued movement restrictions. create a voluntary roster with only necessary contact and accessibility information. assign pairs to safe, authorized areas and establish check in times. use a standard status form: contact made, assistance requested, unable to contact, and referral. escalate medical emergencies to professional responders rather than attempting unsupported interventions. keep personal information confidential and limit sharing to authorized helpers. record completed checks and outstanding requests. safety note: never enter damaged buildings, floodwater, or restricted areas to complete a welfare check.

portable radio readiness inspection confirm handheld radio readiness before deployment. radio & emergency communications verify radio model, charged battery, spare power, antenna, and approved accessories. check that programmed channels match the applicable communications plan. confirm time, location, callsign or identifier, and legal operating authority. perform a brief radio check on an appropriate channel without unnecessary traffic. record receive and transmit performance, battery condition, and faults. pack a paper frequency and contact plan as permitted by the organization. keep radios dry and protect connectors during transport. safety note: never transmit on public safety or other restricted channels without authorization.

paper map and route backup preserve basic navigation when gps or data service fails. navigation & cartography obtain a current paper map covering home, destination, and alternate routes. mark major roads, bridges, known flood areas, shelters, and meeting points. write addresses and phone numbers for destinations on a separate card. practice orienting the map using visible landmarks. check official road closures before travel when information is available. keep maps in a protective sleeve and a spare copy in the vehicle. revisit routes after construction, seasonal flooding, or other changes. safety note: never cross barricades or drive through floodwater based on a paper route plan.

portable power bank rotation keep backup charging equipment serviceable. power generation & electricity list power banks by capacity, supported ports, and assigned device. inspect cases, cables, and connectors for damage or swelling. charge and store according to the manufacturer’s temperature and state of charge guidance. test charging with each essential device and note compatible cables. label each bank with its last inspection date. rotate units so one remains ready for immediate use. dispose of damaged lithium batteries through appropriate collection channels. safety note: do not use, puncture, or charge swollen, leaking, or overheating batteries.

document backup and offline access preserve important reference files during a connectivity outage. computing & offline information systems identify documents needed for immediate decisions, including contacts, plans, maps, and manuals. store a working copy on a device that can open files without internet access. create a second copy on separate removable storage or another trusted device. encrypt sensitive records where appropriate and keep recovery information secure. test opening the files while the device is disconnected from all networks. record backup date, storage location, and responsible custodian. refresh copies when important information changes. safety note: a file being visible in a cloud app does not guarantee offline availability; test actual access.

documenting essential household records create a portable reference to critical household information. family & household continuity list identification, insurance, property, financial, and emergency contact records needed during displacement. keep originals secured; prepare copies only when lawful and appropriate. store digital copies in an encrypted location and protect access credentials separately. include policy numbers and provider contact details without recording passwords in the document. maintain a paper contact sheet in a sealed, water resistant sleeve. identify an authorized person who can retrieve records if the primary custodian is unavailable. review after moves, policy renewals, and household changes. do not include personal record copies in shared or public article modules.

neighborhood welfare check planning organize voluntary checks after a disruption without exposing volunteers to hazards. emergency management & community response identify neighbors who have opted in to being contacted and record preferred communication methods privately. establish a check sequence that begins with phone or radio before any physical visit. assign pairs when conditions permit and tell a coordinator where each pair is going. avoid entering damaged buildings, floodwater, downed wire areas, or locations restricted by responders. ask whether immediate assistance or emergency services are needed; do not diagnose conditions. record contact time, response, urgent needs, and any referral using minimal personal information. escalate life threatening situations to emergency services when available. close the loop by confirming that requested assistance was delivered or handed off.

plain language radio message format use a repeatable structure to pass accurate short radio messages. radio & emergency communications identify the intended recipient and your station according to the rules of the radio service. state whether the message is emergency, priority, or routine without misusing distress calls. give the location with a recognizable reference and repeat coordinates when accuracy matters. describe the observed situation, time of observation, and whether the information is firsthand. state the requested action and any relevant deadline. read back critical numbers, addresses, and instructions for confirmation. log the time, sender, recipient, and disposition of the message. follow applicable licensing, frequency, and emergency traffic procedures.

radio battery rotation and charging log keep portable radios available during prolonged power interruptions. radio & emergency communications inventory each radio and battery by a unique local label. record battery chemistry and use only a charger intended for that pack. check for swelling, leaks, heat damage, and damaged contacts; isolate suspect packs safely. set a routine to check charge state without repeatedly deep discharging batteries. prioritize charging for radios assigned to active duty and emergency monitoring. keep spare packs cool and dry within manufacturer storage limits. log charging start, finish, observed faults, and next inspection date. do not charge damaged batteries or leave improvised charging systems unattended.

portable power bank inventory track available stored energy and prioritize essential devices. power generation & electricity list each power bank by capacity, connector type, and supported output ratings. record which critical devices each bank can actually charge. test cables and adapters before an outage. label dedicated banks for communications, lighting, and accessibility equipment. recharge and inspect according to manufacturer instructions. keep lithium batteries away from excessive heat, water, and puncture hazards. track estimated remaining charge rather than assuming nameplate capacity equals usable energy. never use damaged, swollen, or overheating packs.

accessible evacuation communication cards prepare concise instructions that support communication and reunification. family & household continuity ask each person what information they want responders or helpers to know. include preferred name, communication method, and emergency contact details with consent. describe essential equipment or support needs in simple, actionable terms. use large readable print and symbols where useful. include a current date and an instruction to verify information when possible. keep one copy with the person and another with their designated caregiver where appropriate. protect privacy and avoid placing unnecessary medical details on publicly visible cards. practice using the card during a household evacuation drill.

post storm exterior inspection from a safe distance recognize hazards before approaching a damaged property. natural disasters & environmental hazards wait for official clearance and avoid traveling through restricted or flooded areas. observe the building from a safe location before approaching. look for sagging roofs, leaning walls, broken glass, hanging branches, and unstable debris. assume every downed wire is energized; keep away and report it to the utility or emergency services. do not enter standing water near electrical equipment. if you smell gas or hear a leak, leave the area and contact the utility or emergency services from safety. photograph visible damage only when it can be done without approaching hazards. seek a qualified inspection before reentering a building with structural or electrical damage.

clean water container labeling prevent confusion between potable, untreated, and utility water. water collection & treatment choose food grade containers appropriate for drinking water. clean and sanitize containers using current public health guidance before filling. label each container clearly as drinking water, untreated water, or nonpotable utility water. add fill date and source to the label. keep caps and dispensing tools clean and avoid touching the inside of openings. store away from fuels, chemicals, direct sunlight, and extreme heat. use a separate scoop or spigot for untreated water to prevent cross contamination. if water safety is uncertain, follow current local health authority treatment instructions before drinking.

handwashing station setup during water interruptions provide a dedicated handwashing location when normal plumbing is unavailable. water, waste & public sanitation choose a stable surface away from food preparation and drinking water storage. provide a clean water container with a controlled pour or spigot, soap, and a catch basin. label the station for handwashing and keep untreated water separate. arrange drainage or collection so wastewater does not pool or contaminate living areas. wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, including between fingers and under nails. prioritize washing after toilet use, before food preparation, and after handling waste. empty wastewater into an approved disposal location according to local instructions. refill and clean the station routinely; avoid shared standing wash water.

refrigerator and freezer temperature log use measured temperatures to inform food safety decisions during outages. food & nutrition keep an appliance thermometer in the refrigerator and freezer before an outage. record the time power failed and keep doors closed as much as possible. log actual thermometer readings and times rather than estimating from how food feels. a refrigerator should generally remain at or below 40°f and a freezer at 0°f or below during normal operation. follow usda and fda outage guidance when deciding whether perishable foods must be discarded. do not taste food to determine safety; appearance and odor alone are unreliable. discard food exposed to floodwater or other contamination. when in doubt about safety, discard the item rather than risk illness.

paper map annotation for evacuation routes prepare usable route references when electronic navigation is unavailable. navigation & cartography obtain a current regional road map and identify the map edition or date. mark primary and alternate destinations with clear symbols. highlight routes while preserving printed road names and legends. mark bridges, low water crossings, and other known constraints without assuming they will remain passable. record official evacuation zone and shelter information separately so it can be updated. add fuel, rest, and accessibility stops as planning references, not guaranteed services. store the map in a protective sleeve with a pencil. use official closures and evacuation instructions over a preplanned route.

two minute household departure check use a short checklist before leaving during a time sensitive evacuation. emergency survival & decision making follow immediate evacuation orders and do not delay departure to complete a checklist. account for people and essential mobility or medical support items. take keys, phones, necessary medications, and accessible emergency information if already at hand. check that required assistance for children, pets, and dependent adults is assigned. use the safest available exit and avoid elevators during fire emergencies. do not reenter to retrieve forgotten possessions. tell an out of area contact where the household is heading when safe. confirm arrival and update the contact if the destination changes.

indoor shelter area selection choose a safer interior location for applicable severe weather hazards. shelter & environmental protection identify the hazard first; tornado, hurricane, flood, fire, and chemical incidents require different shelter decisions. for tornado warnings, use a small interior room on the lowest safe floor, away from windows. do not shelter in a basement when flooding is occurring or expected. keep an accessible route for all household members. move away from glass, large unsupported roof spans, and exterior doors when appropriate. store flashlights, sturdy footwear, and communication devices nearby. use official alerts for shelter instructions and evacuation orders. reassess if water enters, smoke develops, or the structure becomes unsafe.

volunteer assignment board track who is doing what without exposing sensitive information. emergency management & community response create columns for task, location, assigned person, check in time, and status. use simple statuses such as pending, assigned, active, and complete. prioritize life safety tasks and route hazardous work to qualified responders. record task limitations, required equipment, and communication method. give each team a check in interval and an escalation contact. do not post medical details or private addresses on a publicly visible board. close tasks only after the receiving person confirms completion. archive completed assignments for the after action review.

offline document backup verification confirm that an emergency reference archive can actually be opened. computing & offline information systems list the files and applications needed to read critical information. copy the archive to a second storage device using the operating system file manager. open a representative sample of documents from the backup device, not the original. check that file names and folder structures remain understandable offline. record the backup date and device label. keep a second copy in a separate safe location when practical. protect sensitive data using appropriate encryption and access controls. repeat the test after major updates and before storm season.

daily incident activity log capture decisions and observations in chronological order. field tools, calculators & forms start each page with the date, time zone, incident name, and recorder. use a consistent time format for all entries. record significant observations separately from assumptions or reports from others. include the source and time received for secondhand information. document decisions, assigned actions, and expected follow up. correct mistakes with a dated note rather than silently deleting history. keep private personal information to the minimum required. transfer or secure the log at shift change.

household check in during extended disruptions maintain clear expectations and identify emerging support needs. psychological resilience & group dynamics choose a predictable short check in time each day. ask each person about immediate needs, concerns, and available energy without requiring disclosure. explain known facts, uncertainties, and the next planned update. assign manageable tasks that match each person’s abilities and preferences. make space for rest, quiet, and private time. avoid spreading unverified rumors or alarming speculation. identify when professional medical or crisis support is needed and seek it when available. record practical follow up actions without documenting unnecessary personal disclosures.

vehicle readiness before evacuation season inspect basic supplies and service status before travel is urgent. transportation & vehicle maintenance review fuel or charge range and identify realistic refueling alternatives. check tire condition and pressure when tires are cold, using the vehicle placard. verify lights, wipers, windshield fluid, and mirrors. check service reminders and address safety critical defects with a qualified mechanic. keep registration, insurance, and roadside contact details accessible. load appropriate water, charging cables, first aid supplies, and a flashlight. plan for passengers, child restraints, accessibility needs, and pets. never run a vehicle engine in a garage or enclosed space.

carbon monoxide alarm inspection check that carbon monoxide warning devices are present and functioning. fire, heating & cooking systems identify every installed carbon monoxide alarm and its manufacturer instructions. confirm placement and replacement dates according to applicable codes and manufacturer guidance. use the test button as directed; it does not verify sensor calibration. replace batteries or the entire alarm when indicated by the manufacturer. never use fuel burning generators, grills, or camp stoves indoors or in attached garages. if an alarm sounds, move everyone to fresh air immediately and contact emergency services. do not reenter until responders or qualified personnel say it is safe. record inspection dates and replacement needs.

field clothing layer inventory match spare clothing to expected conditions and individual needs. wilderness skills & natural resources list expected temperature, rain, wind, and exposure duration for the operating area. choose a moisture managing base layer, insulating layer, and protective outer layer as conditions require. keep spare socks and dry clothing protected in a waterproof bag. check fit and mobility with equipment already worn. include gloves, head covering, and sun protection where appropriate. avoid relying on cotton clothing for insulation when wet in cold conditions. inspect items for damage and replace worn weather protection. reassess clothing requirements as forecasts and seasons change.

a ten-minute household situation briefing turn scattered observations into a short action plan with named responsibilities, explicit uncertainty, and a scheduled reassessment. emergency survival & decision making purpose and limits: use this briefing when a disruption begins and household members need a shared picture. it is a coordination method, not a reason to delay evacuation, emergency calls, or urgent medical care. if the current location is unsafe, move to a safer place first when a safe route is available. do not enter a hazardous area to complete the worksheet. prepare a single record: put the date, time, location, and recorder at the top of a page. divide it into people, immediate hazards, essential services, resources, and next decisions. use a pencil and a clock that everyone can reference. if people are separated, record confirmed locations separately from assumed ones; a missed check-in is not confirmation of injury or safety. describe observations before conclusions: ask each person what they directly saw, where, and when. write “water crossing the driveway at 14:10” instead of “the neighborhood is flooding.” label secondhand reports with the speaker and time received. unknown facts deserve an explicit question mark. this prevents a repeated rumor from quietly becoming an instruction. choose the next three actions: identify the tasks that reduce immediate exposure or maintain essential care. give each task one responsible adult, a safe boundary, and a check-back time. “contact the utility and report back in ten minutes; do not approach the downed line” is more useful than “check the electricity.” do not assign anyone work beyond their training, mobility, or available protection. set decision triggers: record what would make you leave, stop a task, request help, or change destinations. use official instructions and site-specific conditions rather than invented universal thresholds. agree on where people will regroup if communications fail. a trigger is only usable if someone is actually monitoring it and knows how to inform the group. reassess and hand over: read the three actions aloud, ask each owner to repeat their task, and set the next briefing time. at the next briefing, distinguish completed work, changed conditions, and unresolved needs. keep earlier pages rather than erasing the history. a replacement recorder should be able to identify the current plan without relying on someone's memory.

assemble and maintain a usable first-aid kit organize basic supplies around familiar tasks, personal needs, inspection, and the limits of your training. medical care & first aid scope: a first-aid kit supports trained care; possessing equipment does not qualify someone to diagnose an illness or perform a procedure. this guide covers preparation and organization, not treatment or medication dosing. for serious injury, breathing difficulty, altered consciousness, or another urgent concern, seek emergency medical help through locally available channels. start with the people and setting: record how many people the kit supports, the time needed to reach professional care, common activities, and known accessibility requirements. ask household members about essential personal items they want included, while respecting privacy. for prescriptions, storage-sensitive products, and individual medical plans, obtain advice from the relevant clinician or pharmacist rather than improvising substitutions. build a simple inventory: a commercially prepared kit can be a starting point. group unopened dressings, protective gloves, hygiene supplies, and other familiar items into labeled pouches. add a printed inventory with quantity, expiration where applicable, location, and replenishment contact. keep instructions for unfamiliar products with their packaging. exclude items no one can safely use, and store sharps or medicines so children cannot access them. keep clean work clean: place the kit somewhere dry and reachable without entering a hazard. keep it separate from cleaning chemicals, food waste, and repair materials. cdc identifies handwashing before and after treating a wound as an important hygiene practice. plan access to soap and safe running water; alcohol-based sanitizer of at least 60% alcohol is a fallback when soap and water are unavailable, not a substitute for every situation. inspect and replenish: open the kit on a clean surface before a trip and after use. check package seals, contamination, moisture, missing items, and expiration dates. follow manufacturers' storage instructions; a car can expose supplies to temperature extremes. replace compromised products rather than attempting to sterilize disposable materials at home. record what was used without storing unnecessary medical details in a public inventory. practice the retrieval task: ask a second person to find the kit and a named pouch without coaching. correct confusing labels or blocked access. pair the kit with current hands-on first-aid training and local emergency contacts. at the next review, prioritize the gaps revealed by actual use instead of adding increasingly complex equipment.

build a weather-ready personal shelter kit choose, pack, and practice with a shelter system before exposure makes experimentation costly. shelter & environmental protection scope and safe location: this is a preparation guide for a personal shelter kit, not a construction specification or a guarantee against extreme weather. evacuation orders, fire, flooding, unstable trees, and damaged structures can make an otherwise comfortable shelter location unacceptable. choose a legal, safe location first; do not treat a tarp as protection from every environmental hazard. match the kit to conditions: list the coldest, wettest, and windiest conditions realistically expected for the place and season. consider ground moisture, insects, mobility, and how a person will keep clothing dry. the national park service includes extra clothing and emergency shelter in its ten essentials. a tent, bivy, tarp, or emergency blanket has different limitations; read the manufacturer's instructions and do not assume interchangeable performance. check the complete system: lay out shelter fabric, poles or supports, stakes where permitted, cordage appropriate to the product, ground protection, insulation, and a light. inspect seams, fasteners, poles, and anchor points. a missing connector can make a larger component useless. pack small repair items only if you know how to use them, and avoid tying anything to an unsafe overhead object. practice in forgiving conditions: erect the shelter in daylight near a safe indoor fallback. time the task, then repeat it with gloves or the lighting you expect to use. confirm that the occupants fit, entry and exit remain accessible, and the fabric is not pressed against hot equipment. dry the components completely before repacking so the practice does not create a moisture problem in storage. separate shelter from combustion: never run a generator inside a tent, building, garage, or other enclosure. cdc warns that camp stoves and charcoal are unsafe indoors; do not improvise a heater by burning fuel in your sleeping space. keep the shelter plan compatible with safe cooking arrangements rather than trading exposure risk for carbon-monoxide or fire risk. write the fallback plan: put the shelter model, missing parts, packing location, last practice date, and known limits on a kit card. identify what would cause you to seek a building, cancel a trip, or leave the area. a successful practice includes recognizing when the kit is insufficient and acting before weather removes the safer alternatives.

boil and protect emergency drinking water follow a clear heat-treatment workflow for microbial contamination while recognizing hazards boiling cannot remove. water collection & treatment scope and stop conditions: boiling is a method for killing germs. it does not make water contaminated with fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive material safe. if such contamination is known or suspected, use commercially bottled water or another safe source and contact the health department for advice. follow the current local advisory; a “do not use” notice is different from a boil-water notice. prepare a clean workflow: gather a heat-safe pot, a safe heat source, a timer, and clean sanitized containers with tight covers. separate untreated water and its utensils from the finished-water area. keep children and people with limited mobility clear of hot surfaces. do not operate outdoor-only combustion equipment inside to make boiling possible. clarify cloudy water first: cdc advises filtering cloudy water through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter, or allowing it to settle and drawing off the clear portion. this removes visible material; it is not itself disinfection. avoid reintroducing sediment when transferring the clearer water. keep enough volume in the pot for safe handling and leave room to prevent boil-over. apply the boil time: bring the clear water to a rolling boil for one minute. at elevations above 6,500 feet, cdc specifies three minutes. start timing after the water reaches a rolling boil, not while it is merely warming or showing small bubbles. do not mix an untreated batch into a finished batch and assume the earlier boiling time covers both. cool and protect: allow the boiled water to cool without adding untreated water or untreated ice. transfer it using clean handling into sanitized, tightly covered containers. mark the contents as treated and record the preparation date. avoid touching the inside of the container or lid, and pour water out instead of repeatedly dipping hands or a shared cup into it. use safe water consistently: during an applicable advisory, drinking is not the only exposure route. cdc also lists brushing teeth, washing or preparing food, making ice, and other hygiene tasks as activities requiring safe water. follow specific guidance for infant feeding and people with medical needs. a small container reserved for safe-water tasks can reduce accidental use of the wrong supply. if you cannot boil: use safe bottled water when available. chemical treatment depends on product concentration, contact time, water conditions, and the organisms of concern; follow the product label and public-health guidance rather than an improvised dose. portable filters do not all remove bacteria, parasites, and viruses. a clear appearance or improved taste does not establish that water is safe.

make a refrigerator-outage decision record use time and temperature evidence to make conservative food decisions without tasting questionable food. food & nutrition purpose: during a power failure, a short written record helps distinguish measured conditions from guesses. this guide follows cdc's general emergency food guidance; it does not override food-specific instructions, medical dietary needs, or local public-health orders. never taste food to decide whether it is safe, and do not assume reheating reverses every hazard created by unsafe storage. prepare before the outage: keep appliance thermometers in the refrigerator and freezer. cdc specifies 40°f or below for the refrigerator and 0°f or below for the freezer. have an insulated cooler and frozen gel packs if practical. record where thermometers are placed and how you will read them without repeatedly opening the doors. an inaccessible or unreadable thermometer provides little decision support. begin the record: write the known or estimated time power was lost, the last reliable temperature, the time of each check, and whether doors were opened. label uncertain times as estimates. keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible. with doors closed, cdc gives general holding periods of four hours for a refrigerator, 48 hours for a full freezer, and 24 hours for a half-full freezer. plan the cold-source transition: if the outage reaches four hours and a cooler and ice are available, move refrigerated perishables to the cooler and keep them at 40°f or below. record the time and measured conditions. the fact that a container contains ice is not by itself proof that every food inside has stayed cold enough; placement, meltwater, opening, and duration affect the result. decide conservatively: cdc advises discarding refrigerated perishables such as meat, fish, eggs, milk, cut produce, and leftovers after four hours without power or a cold source. use the current food-specific discard chart when an item needs a more precise decision. thawed frozen food that still contains ice crystals or is at 40°f or below may be refrozen or cooked according to cdc's guidance. if a safe history cannot be established, discard it. separate disposal from recovery: mark questionable food so it is not accidentally served while someone seeks advice. keep discarded material away from animals and children. floodwater exposure creates additional contamination concerns even when a package looks intact; do not treat a temperature record as a flood-safety assessment. preserve the record for planning future cold-storage capacity, not as a justification for taking a chance on uncertain food.

start a small vegetable bed with a planting log choose manageable crops, prepare suitable soil, and use local conditions rather than a borrowed calendar. agriculture & gardening scope: a first vegetable bed should teach reliable production at a scale you can water, weed, and observe. it will not immediately replace stored food or a complete diet. the cited university of minnesota guidance is region-specific; its planting dates and crop choices are not universal. use local extension advice, your growing season, and current weather to adapt the plan. choose the site and scale: mark a small accessible area with suitable sunlight and a dependable water source. check access rules and whether past land use suggests contamination. where soil history is uncertain, obtain appropriate local advice and testing rather than assuming an attractive site is safe for food production. leave room to reach plants without repeatedly stepping on the growing area. prepare soil at the right moisture: minnesota extension advises avoiding soil work when it is too wet or too dry. soil that sticks heavily to a shovel is too wet; appropriately moist soil crumbles rather than remaining a tight molded ball. use a soil test to guide amendments and fertilizer. more amendment is not automatically better, and an improvised fertilizer dose can damage plants or nearby water. select a short crop list: choose crops you already eat and can use after harvest. read the seed packet for spacing, depth, temperature requirements, maturity time, and whether the crop is better direct-sown or transplanted. separate cool-season and warm-season decisions. a favorable afternoon is not evidence that the soil or remaining season meets a crop's requirements. plant and label: record crop, variety, seed lot if available, date, location, and what was planted. mark rows so later weeding does not remove seedlings. water gently enough to avoid washing seeds out. if using transplants, acclimate them to outdoor conditions before moving them permanently; do not reduce water to the point of wilting or ignore a frost forecast. observe and adjust: make brief regular entries for emergence, rainfall or watering, visible damage, and harvest. describe symptoms before guessing the cause. use a local extension service for pest or disease identification and follow any product label exactly. at season's end, compare effort and harvest, keep successful varieties in the plan, and expand only as water, labor, and storage allow.

prepare an animal evacuation information packet keep care instructions, identification, transport arrangements, and veterinary contacts together before displacement. animal husbandry & fisheries scope: this packet is intended for household pets and must be adapted with a veterinarian or appropriate animal professional for each species. livestock, aquatic systems, exotic animals, and working animals can require specialist transport and facilities. it does not provide sedation, medication changes, or emergency treatment instructions. identify each animal: make a separate sheet with name, species, distinguishing features, a recent photograph, microchip or identification details where applicable, and your contact information. keep ownership and vaccination records as needed by receiving facilities. do not expose sensitive household details on a public lost-animal poster; maintain a private care copy and a limited public identification copy. record ordinary care clearly: document usual food, feeding schedule, water arrangements, equipment, and relevant health needs. include veterinarian contact details and instructions already provided by that veterinarian. keep medicines in their original labeled containers and confirm storage and refill arrangements before a disruption. never give one animal another animal's prescription or substitute a human medicine based on this packet. plan transport and reception: identify a usable carrier, crate, leash, harness, or other species-appropriate restraint and verify it is sound. confirm that the vehicle and receiving site can accommodate the animal. a general evacuation shelter may not house pets in the same way as people; contact the actual facility when possible and keep a fallback destination. practice loading in calm conditions without forcing a distressed animal into a dangerous struggle. handle disruption carefully: cdc notes that even normally gentle pets may behave differently when frightened or injured. keep pets restrained during transport and away from wildlife, strays, contaminated water, and damaged areas. wash hands after handling animals, their food, or waste. seek veterinary help for illness or injury and report bite wounds to medical personnel promptly. keep the packet current: store a printed copy with transport supplies and a protected digital copy where appropriate. when returning home, inspect for sharp debris, chemicals, damaged wiring, and escape routes before releasing an animal into the area. record what changed during evacuation so temporary caretakers do not rely on outdated instructions.

pack a short-trip kit as ten separate systems check a day-outing pack by function, then practice using it before extending the trip. wilderness skills & natural resources purpose: a system-based pack check reduces the chance that a familiar object is present but unusable. the national park service's ten essentials is a starting framework, not a universal packing list. weather, terrain, remoteness, activity, group needs, and site rules may require additional equipment, specialist training, or cancellation. write a modest trip plan: record the intended route, start time, expected return, companions, and who will act if you do not check in. leave the plan with a responsible contact. download or print location-specific information while connected. do not turn the availability of a navigation device into an assumption that a closed route, flood crossing, or technical terrain is safe. check the first five functions: navigation requires an appropriate map and a tool you know how to use; carry a physical backup. sun protection should address skin and eyes. extra clothing should match the worst plausible conditions rather than only the departure temperature. illumination needs a working light and compatible spare power. first-aid supplies must suit the group and remain within the users' training. check the remaining functions: the nps framework also includes fire, repair tools, extra food, hydration with appropriate water treatment, and emergency shelter. fire equipment must remain compatible with local restrictions and safe conditions; carrying it is not permission to light a fire. choose repairs you can perform, food that requires little preparation, and a shelter you have actually set up. test the dependencies: turn the light on, inspect battery contacts, open the map, and check that water-treatment instructions are legible. verify that a charging lead fits both the power source and the device. a packed stove without an appropriate fuel supply or a filter without a serviceable element does not meet its intended function. keep essential items reachable without unloading the entire bag in rain. conduct a low-consequence rehearsal: walk a familiar short route with a safe return option. note discomfort, inaccessible items, unreadable instructions, and equipment you cannot use confidently. correct those issues before increasing distance or exposure. if conditions exceed the plan or someone becomes unwell, turn back or seek help early rather than trying to prove that the pack can compensate.

make a portable-generator safety and load plan separate carbon-monoxide prevention, electrical compatibility, and fuel handling before a generator is needed. power generation & electricity scope and immediate danger: a portable generator can cause fatal carbon-monoxide poisoning, fire, or electrical injury. this planning guide does not authorize building wiring or provide connection instructions for a panel. use manufacturer documentation and a qualified electrician for approved installation arrangements. if a co alarm sounds or poisoning is suspected, move to fresh air immediately and call emergency services; do not remain inside to diagnose the source. choose a safe operating location: cdc says generators must operate outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors, and vents. never run one inside a home or garage, even with doors and windows open. consider neighboring openings as well as your own, changing wind, and whether exhaust could collect. an open shed or partially enclosed space is not a substitute for the required outdoor location. plan detection and supervision: install battery-operated or battery-backup co detectors near sleeping areas according to their instructions. test and replace them as the manufacturer directs. co is colorless and odorless; a lack of smell does not establish safety. headache, dizziness, weakness, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion can be signs of poisoning, but an absence of symptoms is not a reliable monitoring method. prepare the load list: for each intended appliance, record the exact model, manufacturer-rated power requirements, startup requirements where specified, and the priority of the need. compare the combined requirements with the generator's documented continuous and surge limits. do not infer compatibility from plug fit or invent a starting-watt multiplier. life-support or temperature-sensitive medical equipment requires its own professional continuity plan. keep connections within instructions: do not feed power into a household outlet or improvise a connection to building wiring. arrange any transfer equipment through a qualified electrician. use only compatible equipment and cords rated for the intended conditions and load; keep damaged cords out of service. water and electrical equipment create additional hazards that require a manufacturer-approved solution, not a homemade enclosure around a running generator. plan fuel and shutdown: follow the generator's instructions for fuel, cooling, refilling, maintenance, and storage. keep fuel away from ignition sources and never refuel hot or running equipment. put the location, load order, inspection notes, and responsible operator on a printed card. a generator that cannot be positioned or connected safely should remain off while you use another continuity option.

document building damage without entering an unsafe structure create a useful observation record for occupants, owners, insurers, and qualified assessors while maintaining a clear no-entry boundary. construction & structural repair scope: this guide covers observation and documentation from a location already known to be safe. it is not a structural inspection, a re-entry clearance, or a repair specification. leaning walls, displaced foundations, sagging roofs, fallen masonry, gas odor, damaged electrical equipment, and official exclusion notices are reasons to stay away and contact the appropriate authority or qualified professional. define the boundary: identify a safe place from which to observe without crossing damaged ground, debris, standing water, or utility hazards. keep people away from the potential fall area; do not approach a visibly unstable feature just to improve a photograph. follow emergency-service instructions and property-access rules. no photograph is worth entering a building whose safety is uncertain. build an observation log: record date, time, observer, viewing location, weather, and which side of the structure is visible. give each photograph a simple identifier that matches the log. describe visible changes such as “new diagonal crack above the north window” rather than stating that a foundation has failed. record approximate dimensions only if they can be observed safely, and label estimates as estimates. preserve context: take a wider view before a detail view from the same safe position. include permanent landmarks that help an assessor identify the location later. keep original files with their timestamps and avoid editing away important context. make copies for sharing and retain an unaltered set; avoid posting identifiable household information publicly. communicate the limit: tell recipients where you stood and which areas you could not see. “no damage visible from the street” is not equivalent to “the building is safe.” keep utility shutdowns, roof access, temporary supports, and structural alterations out of an untrained observer's task list. those actions can create new hazards and need the relevant professional or authority. track the decision: record whom you contacted, what instructions they gave, and whether those instructions restrict access. put the latest access decision in a clearly dated place. do not remove a closure notice or allow a familiar occupant's confidence to substitute for a qualified assessment.

create a repair job card before taking equipment apart record symptoms, safe isolation requirements, parts, and stop points so a repair does not become an undocumented experiment. mechanical systems & fabrication scope: a repair job card supports work you are already competent and authorized to perform. it does not supply a machine-specific isolation procedure or permission to defeat a guard. electrical systems, stored pressure, springs, elevated loads, hot surfaces, fuel, and rotating components can remain hazardous after a switch is turned off. if the necessary isolation and verification are unknown, label the equipment out of service and seek qualified help. capture the symptom: record equipment identity, model, serial number, operating context, last successful use, and exactly what changed. distinguish an observation from a proposed cause. a stopped pump may have several causes; writing “motor failure” too early can lead to unnecessary disassembly. note unusual sounds, indications, leaks, and recent maintenance without energizing unsafe equipment to reproduce them. gather the right information: obtain the correct manual, service limits, part diagram, and required tools. record the manual revision and any consumables needed. confirm that replacement parts match the actual model rather than only appearing similar. set a clean work area where small parts can be contained, and arrange safe handling for heavy or awkward components. record a safe work boundary: identify who may perform the work and the manufacturer-approved isolation process they will follow. include the verification step and who is responsible for preventing unexpected operation. do not use this generic card as a substitute for lockout requirements, site procedures, or hands-on training. uncertainty about stored energy is a stop condition. keep the assembly trail: if disassembly is permitted, take photographs and label removable parts by sequence and orientation. use containers rather than leaving hardware loose. write down observations as they occur. do not assume that an extra washer, seal, spacer, or guard is optional, and do not invent torque values or clearances where the manufacturer specifies them. close with a controlled result: reassembly, inspection, and testing must follow the equipment's documented procedure. record which checks passed, any remaining fault, and whether the equipment is released or still out of service. a machine that runs briefly is not automatically safe. save the job card so the next person knows what was actually changed.

set up a low-water handwashing station arrange safe water, soap, drainage, and a clear cleaning routine where ordinary plumbing is interrupted. water, waste & public sanitation purpose: a handwashing station should make proper washing easy without contaminating the stored clean water. it supports household hygiene during a service interruption;
